entries.title: Dear Congressional Republicans: Your letter to the WNBA isn’t helping anyone
entries.summary: <p>LOS ANGELES — Dear Members of the Republican Study Committee,</p><p>I cover the WNBA for the Chicago Sun-Times. This morning, during my daily women’s basketball news sweep, I came across your letter to Commissioner Cathy Engelbert about Caitlin Clark.</p><p>You begin by stating the obvious: Clark's immense popularity has been good for league business.</p><p>You also acknowledge, in a twisted and disingenuous way, something many players and league stakeholders agree on: WNBA officiating is inconsistent and too often fails to address rough play.</p><p>Then comes the culture-war rallying cry. You assert that the “attacks” against Clark are “racially motivated,” linking to “reports” and “posts” that, somewhat hilariously, don’t work when you try to click them.</p><p>By the end, though, you retreat into safer territory. Although the entire letter centers Clark, your actual demands to Engelbert are strikingly general. You ask about the league’s review mechanism for violence, accountability for overly aggressive actions and protections against online harassment.</p><p>Don’t worry — I didn’t miss the stereotypes or the not-so-subtle pathologizing of a league full of Black women as uniquely violent and in need of special mechanisms to keep that violence in check.</p><p>But I also found the hedge telling. Maybe even you recognized how unserious it sounds for members of Congress to intervene in a professional sports league on behalf of one player.</p><p>Especially when that player has never said she believes she’s the target of racially motivated attacks. Especially when Clark has repeatedly noted that she’s one of many players who’ve been on the wrong end of flagrant fouls.</p><p>After reading your letter, I took an Uber to the Sparks’ shootaround and spoke with Nneka Ogwumike, the president of the players’ union. She found the letter unfortunate, though not particularly surprising.</p><p>Ogwumike said she’s been having plenty of conversations with players about officiating. Increasingly, though, those conversations are also about the vitriol surrounding the league and the people attempting to use it to push their own agendas.</p><p>“The stigmas and the stereotypes and the racism and the bigotry that is tied to the players that we have in this league … it’s incredibly disappointing,” she said. “I guess it’s going to be on us as players to try and see what we can do. But we’re out here playing the games.</p><p>“With women’s sports, these are problems that we don’t create, that we are now burdened to solve.”</p><p>Do you see what’s happening here?</p><p>You claim to be protecting women’s sports, but you’re really just handing the league your emotional baggage and asking its players to carry it.</p><p>Players just fought their asses off to negotiate a collective-bargaining agreement that values them closer to what they’re worth. Many <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/07/06/skylar-diggins-caught-off-guard-by-benching-as-tension-builds-with-sky" >are still fighting</a> for basic resources their male counterparts have had for years.</p><p>Now they're having to deal with even louder and more demeaning agendas. </p><p>So on some level, your radar picked up something real. The league's popularity is growing faster than its infrastructure. They're still trying to build the plane while flying it.</p><p>But the reason for that isn’t what you seem to think. It’s decades of underinvestment and indifference about women’s sports from pretty much anyone.</p><p>Where were your letters then?</p><p>Now look — I know you weren’t expecting this letter from me, or probably even a reply from Engelbert. Your letter is an obvious, opportunistic publicity stunt.</p><p>I know that because, if you actually cared about the WNBA, you probably wouldn’t attach a statement claiming that “if it were not for Caitlin Clark the WNBA would still be irrelevant and possibly even defunct.”</p><p>If you cared about officiating, you could read <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/7423584/2026/07/06/wnba-referees-officiating-issues-offseason-task-force/" target="_blank" >recent reporting</a> from The Athletic showing that the entire WNBA ecosystem knows it’s a problem — and that resource constraints are part of what makes it so difficult to solve.</p><p>If you cared about the players, you wouldn’t repeat narratives that expose many of them to even more online abuse.</p><p>And it’s especially hard to take seriously your closing invocation of “strengthening families” and “protecting opportunities for women in sport.”</p><p>Because you sure are ruining an opportunity for a lot of us.</p><p>I grew up playing basketball in Skokie, Illinois and then Grinnell, Iowa, and the game shaped me. I loved it, relished my successes and learned from my failures. </p><p>When my playing career ended, I struggled to find the next version of myself. I’d identified so strongly as a basketball player that I didn’t always know who I was without it.</p><p>I found solace in becoming a fan of women’s basketball, both at the college level and in the WNBA. It gave my former teammates and me a way to keep sharing our love of the game — videos, debates and conversations about what sports had given us: opportunities to lead, lessons in resilience.</p><p>It also gave us a chance to reckon with what sports had taken from us: the ability to slow down, to forgive ourselves, to stop measuring our worth by performance.</p><p>But maybe the best part was simply getting to be fans again. To watch people playing our game and doing things we could only imagine ourselves doing.</p><p>Chelsea Gray’s behind-the-back passes. Paige Bueckers’ impossible fluidity. And yes, our Iowa roots gave us special connection to Clark’s logo threes, too.</p><p>Following the WNBA and its players created a sense of joy, continuation and belonging.</p><p>If there’s one thing you take away from the response to your letter, let it be this:</p><p>This league means something to people.</p><p>It meant something before Clark arrived. It means something during her rise. It will mean something after she’s gone.</p><p>Now picture something precious to you suddenly becoming a prop in someone else’s political fight. Picture people who’ve shown little interest in understanding it deciding it’s useful after all.</p><p>After a while, that starts to wear on you.</p><p>That’s why I’m writing back.</p><p>That, and the Sky canceled their shootaround this morning, leaving me short of my usual material.</p><p>Look, bleeding-heart liberals can sniff out a good opportunity, too.</p>

entries.title: Caleb Wilson's 35 points in Summer League debut ring in new Bulls era
entries.summary: <p>LAS VEGAS — Darryn Peterson went down quickly.</p><p>In only the second game of North Carolina’s regular season last November, the Tar Heels and Caleb Wilson sent Peterson — the eventual No. 2 overall pick — back to Lawrence, Kansas, with an 87-74 victory against the Jayhawks.</p><p>Wilson, the eventual No. 4 overall pick by the Bulls, scored 24 points, grabbed seven rebounds and added four steals. Peterson scored a solid 22 points but still lost.</p><p>Then came two showdowns against Duke and eventual No. 3 overall pick Cameron Boozer. But Wilson was only available for one, thanks to a broken right thumb that ended his season early.</p><p>North Carolina won that meeting 71-68, with Wilson scoring 23 points and shooting 8-for-12 from the field. Boozer had 24 points and 11 rebounds, but the Blue Devils suffered their first ACC loss.</p><p>The one game that went under the radar, however, was a preseason exhibition that featured eventual No. 1 overall pick AJ Dybantsa and Wilson. While BYU defeated the Tar Heels, Wilson outplayed Dybantsa, finishing with 22 points, 10 rebounds and three blocks. Dybantsa had 18 points and 10 rebounds.</p><p>Meaningless college stats now that all four players are in the NBA? Don’t try selling Wilson on that because he isn’t buying.</p><p>Wilson isn’t your typical 19-year-old, wide-eyed rookie. He’s definitely not the typical player the Bulls have selected in recent years. That has been clear during the last year, and it was again in his franchise-record 35-point Summer League debut Friday in a 97-96 loss to Boozer and the Grizzlies.</p><p>Even before his first college game last season, Wilson said he was making a list of competitors who had done him wrong in his estimation. That included several players he felt froze him out in the McDonald’s High School All-American Game.</p><p>‘‘I’m just going to keep going out there and killing people,’’ he told a reporter after that game. ‘‘I got the list on my phone, and it’s nowhere near done.’’</p><p>The list remains there — updated, of course — and Wilson hasn’t been shy about who tops it: all three players who were selected before him in the draft last month.</p><p>‘‘You know what happened when I played them, so I don’t really care about the media,’’ Wilson said when he was asked recently about where he ended up in the draft order. ‘‘I’m a competitor, and I get to play them in Summer League, too. So whatever needs to be done to prove I’m on the same level . . . but I’m better.’’</p><p>The NBA did him that favor, scheduling the game Friday against Boozer and the Grizzlies, another Monday against Peterson the Jazz, then one Tuesday against Dybantsa and the Wizards — all of them prime-time games and played on the big stage at the Thomas & Mack Center.</p><p>It’s a chance for Wilson to make an early statement as the changing of the Bulls’ guard continues.</p><p>Give Wilson and Boozer credit because they understood the assignment. In addition to his 35 points, Wilson quieted critics of his outside shooting by going 7-for-11 from three-point range. Boozer, meanwhile, scored 23 points and came away with the victory.</p><p>‘‘Yes, I scored a lot, but we still didn’t win, so I don’t really care,’’ Wilson said afterward. ‘‘[Boozer] is a great player, honestly, one of the few guys I respect out of my class. He played a great game, and he won. We’ll learn from this and get better.’’</p><p>Even before Wilson, guard Dailyn Swain and forward Noa Essengue stepped on the floor to face the Grizzlies, the Bulls made two key additions official.</p><p>The team filled its vacancy in the middle by announcing the trade that was reported two weeks ago, acquiring center Nic Claxton in a four-team deal that included the Nets, Hornets and Timberwolves. The Bulls exercised their option on forward Mouhamadou Gueye and sent him to the Hornets as a part of the deal.</p><p>The Bulls hope the 6-11 Claxton can return to the ultra-athletic rim protector/rim runner he was a few seasons ago before back issues seemingly grounded him. If he can do that, that would give the Bulls a frontcourt of Matas Buzelis, Wilson and Claxton. That’s not exactly a fun group to try to score on.</p><p>The Bulls also made official their two-year, $45 million free-agent signing of guard Norman Powell, with the second year being a team option. That’s significant for several reasons, with the first being the most obvious. The Bulls lost a lot of outside shooting in their roster purge in February, and Powell — fresh off an All-Star season with the Heat — should help in that department.</p><p>Off the court, Powell has a reputation as a no-nonsense veteran who understands the ups and downs of an NBA season. The young Bulls core needs that sort of player in the locker room, and Powell, 33, is made for that role at this point of his career.</p>

entries.title: Shota Imanaga has given up more home runs than just about anyone, but Cubs thankful for what he’s given them
entries.summary: <p>CINCINNATI – <b>Shota Imanaga</b> gave up another home run Friday night.</p><p>It’s nothing new.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>’ lefty starter has allowed 22 homers, more than all but one pitcher in baseball this season.</p><p>He’s been unable to shake that bad habit, bringing up memories of how costly his home-run problem was last postseason, when he allowed three long balls in just 6 2/3 innings of playoff work against the Padres and Brewers.</p><p>The Cubs, though, will choose to look at the positives Imanaga has delivered for an ailing pitching staff.</p><p>He wrapped up his first half with his 19th start of the season in Friday’s 4-0 Cubs loss, the most on the team. His 108 innings are tops on the Cubs’ staff, as well. That work has been a godsend for a rotation otherwise ravaged by injuries.</p><p>“Shota’s been throwing the ball well,” manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> said before Friday’s game. “He had that little three-start stretch where it didn’t go so well. But him and <b>Colin [Rea]</b> have been the guys who have been able to take the ball every fifth day, and we’ve obviously needed that.”</p><p>“I take a lot of honor in being able to go out there every fifth day, sixth day,” Imanaga said through an interpreter after the game. “I learned in the last three years how difficult it is. Obviously, the results are the results, but going out every fifth, sixth day and taking the ball and pitching, that is really difficult. So I do take a lot of pride in that.”</p><p>At least from a results perspective, that bumpy stretch lasted four starts, in which Imanaga allowed 26 runs and 12 homers in 21 2/3 innings.</p><p>But both before (a 2.32 ERA in nine starts) and after (a 2.81 ERA in six starts since), he’s looked like the top-of-the-rotation arm the Cubs have desperately needed him to be.</p><p>With righty <b>Cade Horton</b> done for the season and righty <b>Ben Brown</b> perhaps unlikely to start again this year, the Cubs need someone to fill the ace role.</p><p>Lefty <b>Matthew Boyd</b> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/01/cubs-matthew-boyd-all-star-ace-starting-rotation-pitching-injuries-craig-counsell-pete-crow-armstrong-alex-bregman-thumbs-down" >is an obvious in-house choice</a>. There’s the potential for trade-deadline additions, though No. 1 pitchers have a tendency to come with massive price tags, something <b>Jed Hoyer</b>’s front office shied away from <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2025/07/31/2025-trade-deadline-cubs-prez-jed-hoyer-balks-at-asking-price-for-frontline-starter-adds-four-players" >as recently as last summer</a>.</p><p>So why not Imanaga?</p><p>Maybe that big home-run number is a barrier to ace-dom. If he can’t keep opposing hitters in the yard come October, the Cubs could have an unwanted sequel on their hands.</p><p>But Friday, despite giving up that homer, it was all he gave up, allowing just one run in his five innings.</p><p>“There was a couple starts there where I didn’t perform well. But thanks to the support of my teammates, I’m still here,” Imanaga said. “Looking at the second half, I’m just thinking about, ‘What do I need to do to better myself as a pitcher?’”</p><p><b>Greene machine</b></p><p>Do you remember? The 18th day of September?</p><p>That’s when <b>Hunter Greene</b> threw a one-hit shutout against the Cubs last season.</p><p>Friday night, the Reds righty was at it again, striking out 12 Cubs and holding them to just three hits in seven scoreless innings.</p><p><b>One more and he’s back?</b></p><p>Righty starter <b>Jameson Taillon</b> will make a second minor league rehab start Saturday for Triple-A Iowa, what could be his final tune-up before returning from a hamstring strain that’s kept him on the injured list for more than a month.</p><p>Should everything go well, Counsell said, Taillon will return to the Cubs’ rotation on the other side of the All-Star break.</p><p><b>Swing, batter</b></p><p>Utility man <b>Matt Shaw</b> will test out his sprained hand again this weekend.</p><p>The Cubs are hoping to get Shaw, who has been on the IL since late last month, free of the symptoms he’s experienced in order to get him swinging again after the break.<br></p>

entries.title: White Sox will hold MLB Draft watch party Saturday
entries.summary: <p>The White Sox will hold an MLB Draft party for fans before their 1:10 p.m. game Saturday against the Athletics, but the South Siders still don’t know whom the virtual guest of honor will be.</p><p>The Sox will select first when the draft opens at noon Central time in Philadelphia as a part of All-Star festivities. MLB said Friday no amateur players are scheduled to attend the draft.</p><p>Fans will be able to enter Rate Field at 11:40 a.m.</p><p>There remains no slam-dunk No. 1 pick, but the Sox probably will select one of three players: UCLA shortstop <b>Roch Cholowsky</b>, Texas high school shortstop <b>Grady Emerson</b> or Georgia Tech catcher <b>Vahn Lackey</b>.</p><p>Director of amateur scouting <b>Mike Shirley</b> told reporters Wednesday the Sox still aren’t certain which player they would take.</p><p>The Sox didn’t give any new clues Friday, with most of the pregame discussion centering on the return of slugger <b>Munetaka Murakami</b> six weeks after he suffered a Grade 2 strain of his right hamstring while running to first base in a game against the Tigers.</p><p>The scuttlebutt is that the pick might come down to Cholowsky and Emerson.</p><p>‘‘The Cholowsky-Emerson conversation, the Vahn Lackey conversation, these are real, they are happening,’’ Shirley said. ‘‘You have a catcher and the continuation of these shortstops that continue to define the game across the league. We are searching for this. We’re doing our very absolute best up to the minute to make the best choice.’’</p><p>Cholowsky, 21, is a 6-2 right-handed hitter and was the Big Ten Player of the Year for a second consecutive season. He hit .320 with 21 home runs, 60 RBI and 73 runs scored while starting all 60 of UCLA’s games at shortstop.</p><p>Emerson, 18, is 6-3 and 185 pounds and bats left-handed. He played his senior high school season at Fort Worth Christian High School, where he slashed .532/.648/1.013 with seven homers, 50 RBI and 31 stolen bases.</p><p>Lackey, 21, is a 6-2, 215-pound right-handed hitter who reportedly didn’t receive any Division I offers until his senior year of high school. In his junior season at Georgia Tech, Lackey batted .397 with a 1.291 OPS, 20 homers and 78 RBI in 61 games. He also played third base.</p><p>The Sox already are headed in a much better direction after three consecutive seasons with more than 100 losses.</p><p>‘‘I don’t wanna lose the way we lost to get here; that was painful,’’ Shirley said. ‘‘But how can you not be excited to have the No. 1 pick and with the direction of the club?’’</p><h3>Another Thome on the way?</h3><p><b>Landon Thome</b>, the 18-year-old son of Hall of Famer and former Sox slugger <b>Jim Thome</b>, will be drafted Saturday.</p><p>Landon, an infielder who played at Nazareth Academy in La Grange Park, is ranked as the 34th overall prospect by MILB.com. The 6-foot, 177-pounder is committed to Florida State for next season.</p><p>‘‘All the hard work, which, at the end of the day, they do it all,’’ the elder Thome told MLB Network. ‘‘As a dad, you sit back [and] watch the journey.’’</p><h3>HR derby replacement</h3><p>Former White Sox center fielder <b>Brian Anderson</b> will replace <b>Alexei Ramirez</b> in the Alumni Home Run Derby on Saturday. entries.title: FAA extends flight limits at O'Hare Airport
entries.summary: <p>The Federal Aviation Administration announced Friday it will limit flights out of O’Hare International Airport for another year.</p><p>The FAA had already <a class="Link" href="http://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/04/16/faa-orders-summer-flight-reduction-at-ohare-citing-safety-efficiency" target="_blank" >imposed flight limits earlier this year</a> that were set to remain in place through Oct. 24. Under the order, O’Hare’s daily flights were capped at 2,708 down from the 3,080 daily flights airlines had planned for this summer.</p><p>The order was extended until Oct. 30, 2027.</p><p>The agency said the order was extended because construction projects and airfield adjustments expected to continue through next summer will limit airport capacity and affect operations.</p><p>“FAA finds that significant delay and operational disruption would occur at [O’Hare if the [O’Hare] Order were to expire as originally scheduled,” the agency said in a statement.</p><p>The Chicago Department of Aviation did not immediately respond to a request for comment.<br></p>

entries.title: Funeral services announced for George E. Johnson, founder of Johnson Products Company
entries.summary: <p>Funeral services will be July 17 for George E. Johnson Sr., founder of the Johnson Products Company.</p><p>Johnson’s visitation will take place July 16 from 4 p.m. to 8 p.m. at Leak and Sons Funeral Home, 7838 S. Cottage Grove Ave., according to an announcement from his family. A funeral service will be held July 17 at 11 a.m. at Trinity United Church of Christ, 400 W. 95th St.</p><p>Johnson, who founded Johnson Products Company, which created hair care products tailored to Black consumers, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/obituaries/2026/07/06/george-e-johnson-founder-of-johnson-products-company-dies-at-99" target="_blank" >died Monday morning</a> from natural causes at his Downtown Chicago condo at age 99, according to his son John Edward Johnson. </p><p>Johnson’s company, headquartered at 8522 S. Lafayette Ave., manufactured product lines including Ultra Sheen, Classy Curl, Curly Perm and Black Tie men’s cologne. It was the first Black-owned company to trade on the American Stock Exchange.<br></p>

entries.title: Ammons indictment puts all eyes on Welch
entries.summary: <p>Rep. Luis Arroyo, D-Chicago, was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2019/10/28/20936456/state-rep-luis-arroyo-indicted-public-corruption-charge" >arrested</a> by the FBI on Oct. 28, 2019, for attempting to bribe a state senator. House Speaker Michael Madigan, who was under investigation himself, called on Arroyo to resign that same day.</p><p>The next day, Rep. Emanuel “Chris” Welch, D-Hillside, was one of three House Democrats who signed a petition to automatically trigger the creation of a Special Investigating Committee. Welch and the two others included the sworn federal criminal complaint against Arroyo as evidence.</p><p>Arroyo announced his <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2019/11/1/20943659/luis-arroyo-state-representative-resigns" >resignation</a> just hours before the first investigating committee hearing. He was later sentenced to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2022/5/25/23141317/luis-arroyo-sentencing-wire-fraud-bribery-terry-link-sweepstakes-gambling-machines" >almost five years</a>.</p><p>On Feb. 25 of this year, now Illinois House Speaker Welch, without an announcement, kicked Rep. Harry Benton, D-Plainfield, out of the House Democratic caucus and stripped him of his committee assignments and House staff support.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-780000" name="module-780000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>In April, my colleague Isabel Miller asked Welch if Benton should resign, but he wouldn’t respond. On July 1, Welch announced that he’d received an inspector general’s report and demanded that Benton resign, which <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/07/06/harry-benton-investigation-report-misconduct-illinois-legislature" >Benton did</a> two days later.</p><p>And that brings us to Rep. Carol Ammons, D-Urbana, who was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/07/10/carol-ammons-indictment-illinois-house-harry-benton-resign" >indicted last week</a> by the feds on multiple charges, including paying her daughter more than $15,000 from her campaign fund disguised as a payment to what appears to be a nonexisting consultant, and then allegedly receiving kickbacks.</p><p>Ammons is also accused of killing an appropriation for the Urbana Neighborhood Connections Center and in its place arranging more than $650,000 in the fiscal year 2020 budget for Hood Vote for Neighborhood Transformation — and then her daughter was paid out of that appropriation. Gov. JB Pritzker’s administration figured out what was going on and told Ammons and the group that this was an impermissible conflict of interest. Ammons’ daughter left the payroll.</p><p>The next year, Ammons allegedly inserted a $612,000 grant to Bridgewater-Sullivan Community Life Center into the state budget. Ammons allegedly then assisted the group in drafting the contract to hire her daughter, and allegedly received kickbacks. That same daughter was also paid about $10,000 by the Urbana-Champaign Independent Media Center, which Ammons helped with budgetary member initiatives totaling $700,000 in fiscal year 2021 and fiscal year 2022.</p><p>The feds allege that, in total, Ammons and her daughter received benefits “in excess of $100,000.” The government allegedly has multiple text messages that implicate Ammons. She’s also accused of lying to the FBI when she said she had no knowledge of any conflict of interest with the Hood Vote group.</p><p>Welch told reporters last week that he wouldn’t call for Ammons’ resignation because she has the right to due process. I asked a day later how a still-secret legislative inspector general report would qualify as due process for Benton and a public federal grand jury indictment does not for Ammons. I was told by a Welch spokesperson that the speaker considers the federal indictment akin to Welch’s own referral to the legislative inspector general. And then the adjudication happened during the legislative inspector general’s investigation and report. Seems a bit of a stretch.</p><p>Welch told reporters he’d consider a special investigating committee to be “due process” if members demanded it.</p><p>The special investigation committee can ultimately lead to a House floor vote to expel Ammons.</p><p>However, Welch also told reporters, “I think the courts is the proper place for this. They have the tools available to them, and it's the proper place.”</p><p>Welch had basically the same response when he chaired the special investigative committee looking into Madigan’s operation. But, unlike Ammons, Madigan had not yet been indicted.</p><p>Also, the House voted to expel Rep. Derrick Smith, D-Chicago, after his arrest and before his federal bribery trial. And Gov. Rod Blagojevich was impeached and removed from office before his federal trial. The argument doesn’t really hold water.</p><h3>Trick bag </h3><p>On Friday, Republicans filed paperwork to initiate the investigating committee. Welch appointed members to it that same day.</p><p>And that, finally, brings us to President Donald Trump. We’ve seen serious problems at the U.S. attorney’s office in Chicago the past several months, and in my opinion, believable allegations have been made of politically motivated prosecutions.</p><p>The Ammons indictment was filed by the Central District of Illinois. I’ve seen nothing yet, which indicates that office is having the same problems as the Northern District.</p><p>But an argument will likely be made that this is yet another politically motivated Trump-era indictment and people should wait, particularly after what happened to Sen. Emil Jones, III, D-Chicago. The splashy federal bribery case against him completely fell apart at trial. Lots of folks, from Pritzker on down, had demanded Jones resign when the indictment was issued.</p><p>It also didn’t help matters that, like with the Madigan probe, only House Republicans signed the petition to initiate action against Ammons. It can be portrayed as partisan.</p><p>Ammons says she’s innocent. I doubt she’ll resign. So, Welch is in a bit of a trick bag.</p><p><i>Rich Miller also publishes Capitol Fax, a daily political newsletter, and CapitolFax.com.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-590000" name="module-590000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Sky fall to Sparks, slip further from playoff picture
entries.summary: <p>LOS ANGELES — The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> needed this one. The Sparks entered the game below .500 and were still without leading scorer Kelsey Plum, making this the more manageable stop before the Sky close their road trip against the 15-8 Wings.</p><p>Instead, the Sky lost 102-87, falling to 7-15 and four games behind the eighth and final playoff spot. And they were once again without point guard Skylar Diggins, who hasn't played since <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/07/07/skylar-diggins-and-tyler-marsh-still-not-aligned-after-benching" >being benched on Monday. </a></p><p>"I think they stole one from us today, and credit to them, they played a really great game," guard Jacy Sheldon said. "They want to play fast, we want to play fast, and it got going in their favor tonight."</p><p>All-Star forward Nneka Ogwumike led the Sparks with 25 points, and every member of their starting five scored at least 15.</p><p>Diggins, meanwhile, missed her second consecutive game — officially out with a knee injury. Coach Tyler Marsh said the team doesn't have a timeline for her return, and conversations about her role remain ongoing. A situation that sounds about as murky as their playoff hopes. </p><p>In her absence, the best stretches came from Sheldon and Gabriela Jaquez off the bench. Sheldon scored 10 points in the first quarter, giving the Sky an early jolt. Jaquez finished with 15 points on 6-for-12 shooting, a welcome performance after a tougher stretch for the rookie.</p><p>Kamilla Cardoso and Sydney Taylor also scored in double figures, but Cardoso battled foul trouble and defensive adjustments. Once she started finding baskets inside, the Sparks sent double-teams and forced the ball out of her hands.</p><p>The Sky kept pace for three quarters and scored 87 points, but Marsh thought their offense lacked connectedness and purpose. The Sparks played with a flow and edge the Sky couldn't match.</p><p>"We've been hanging our hat on our fight, on our grit, on our toughness, on our resilience," Marsh said. "I think today we just recognized this wasn't the level of energy that we've approached the last several games with. We gotta recommit to that."</p><p>The Sky can recommit. But again, they're running out of time — with or without Diggins.</p>
